vignette:
Rajan is a 68-year-old South Asian man, divorced, who works part-time for a small nonprofit organization focused on immigrant resettlement services in a mid-sized American city. He came to therapy seven months after being raped by a man he had trusted - a longtime acquaintance who had offered him a ride home after a community fundraising event. What began as a familiar journey through quiet streets ended when the man pulled into an unlit parking structure, locked the doors, and assaulted Rajan with sustained physical force. Throughout the attack, Rajan heard the low mechanical hum of the parking structure's ventilation system, the man's voice issuing low, controlled instructions, and the sound of his own breathing becoming ragged and then, at some point, almost silent. He did not fight back in the way he had always imagined he would. He went somewhere else in his mind. It was this - the stillness of his own body - that would haunt him most in the months that followed.

In the weeks after the assault, Rajan told no one. He returned to his apartment, which he had lived in alone since his divorce several years earlier, and tried to resume his routines. But the apartment, which had once felt like a refuge, had become something else. He found himself unable to sit in any chair that did not face the door, and he began positioning himself with his back pressed against the wall whenever he sat down - at home, in the office breakroom, at the small community meetings his nonprofit organized for newly arrived families. At work, where he helps coordinate housing placements and legal referrals, he began arriving early specifically to secure a seat against the back wall before others arrived. His colleagues noticed but said nothing at first.

Sleep became shallow and vigilant. He lay awake cataloguing sounds - footsteps in the hallway outside his door, the elevator mechanism, a neighbor's key in a lock - certain each time that someone was entering his home. Unexpected loud sounds, a car backfiring outside his office window or a door slamming in the resettlement center, sent a physical jolt through him that he could not suppress or explain to those nearby. Being touched without warning had become unbearable; during a routine moment when a colleague placed a hand briefly on his shoulder to get his attention, Rajan recoiled so sharply that the room fell quiet.

The memories themselves did not arrive as coherent narrative. Instead, they came in fragments - and when they did, Rajan heard things: the ventilation hum, the man's voice, the specific quality of his own altered breathing. He also felt, in his lower abdomen and pelvis, a dull and then sharp pain that had no current physical source his doctor could identify. When asked in the intake session to describe what had happened, he sat for a long time and then said quietly that he knew everything that had occurred but that the words were simply not available to him - as though language itself had been revoked for this particular knowledge.

Over the months, Rajan had come to believe, with a certainty that felt irrefutable, that his response during and after the assault proved he was fundamentally incapable of managing difficulty - that other men, better men, would have acted differently, recovered faster, spoken sooner. He had come to feel that the emotions he once recognized in himself - warmth toward the families he helped resettle, pleasure in small rituals, connection to his adult children with whom he had been slowly rebuilding a relationship after the divorce - were no longer genuinely accessible to him. What frightened him most, sitting in the intake room, was the possibility that this was permanent. He described himself, carefully and without self-pity, as someone who now stood outside ordinary human life looking in, unable to find the door back.

He had begun hurting himself - pressing his forearm against a hot surface, or digging his nails into his palm - not out of a wish to die, he was clear about that, but because the physical sensation briefly interrupted something internal that had become otherwise unmanageable. It was his youngest daughter, visiting unexpectedly and noticing the marks on his arm, who finally insisted he speak to someone. He came to therapy, he said, because he did not want her to watch him disappear.
